seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: I have just arrived here safe and sound. I obtained a special permit from the Austrian authorities from Trieste to the Swiss frontier and stopped here, Zurich being the first big city after Innsbruck. Of course my flat in Trieste is locked up with all my things. I brought only a few things and some MSS. I have not the least idea what I am going to do or where I am going to stay. I should be back in Trieste on 1 October to take up again my position there but it seems it will be impossible for anyone, Austrian or foreigner, to return to that city for a long time. Since the Italian declaration of war life was not at all pleasant there. Here at least I do not hear cannonading every day and we are not exposed to aeroplane raids of which we had four. I suppose you know all this so I shall not write about it. Besides, the subject is rather tiresome – to me, at least, who have been in the midst of it for the last year. But I must say that, so far as I am concerned, Austrian authorities were both now and before during my stay of twelve years obliging and considerate. I have written a card to Miss Weaver and am writing also to Mr Pinker. In the last letter I had from my publisher he sent me an account sales of a few hundred copies on which I get no royalty. A royalty of any kind or amount in the present circumstances would be very useful. I hope there is some prospect of it as I do not know how long I may be obliged to live in Switzerland before the way is clear for me to return to Trieste. Any letters which were sent to me care of my friend in Murano after the Italian declaration of course did not reach me. I have written to my friend there to send on any letters for me but the Italian censorship at Bologna holds up the post, inward and outward, for eight or ten days so that I cannot have a reply very soon. Possibly the English censorship acts more quickly. I had some seven weeks ago or more through Venice letters from New York, about an American edition of “Dubliners ”. Mr Grant Richards however says there is no such edition. I understand nothing of the affair. The only fact that emerges so far as I can see is that I receive nothing.

I suppose my novel has reached its end now. I have written a play Exiles and was engaged on a novel Ulysses
of which I have written the first two episodes. It is a continuation of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man after three years’ interval blended with many of the persons of Dubliners. I shall not finish it soon for many reasons. Your letters nearly always bring me good news so that I look forward to your reply. I hope you are well and in your usual good humour. A letter to this address will reach me certainly.

div.note: Italy’s entry into the Great War in May 1915 and the consequent focus on Trieste at the junction of two enemy nations drove the Joyce family to Zurich where they rode out the duration in safety and relative isolation. With the help of influential pupils, they left Trieste in late June 1915, “by special permission, JJ noted, “of the military authorities when the partial evacuation of the city was decided on” (LI 82). They had safe passage through Austria into Switzerland and settled, initially, at Gasthof Hoffnung (“Inn of Hope”) in Zurich, where they remained until 7 July 1915. JJ and Nora had stayed at the same inn in October 1904 after eloping from Dublin.

After signing the secret Treaty of London and being promised financial aid and large territories to the north of Italy and to the east across the Adriatic, Italy declared war on Austria-Hungary on 23 May 1915, entering on the side of the Allies – Great Britain, France, and Russia.

In late May 1915, newspapers reported that Italian forces were pressing towards Trieste and Gorizia, where Austrian troops awaited them. In nearby Trentino, a large artillery battle took place as Italian and Austrian troops clashed in the Tyrolean Alps. Italian aviators were active along the front, dropping bombs near Trieste and damaging the railway between Nabresina (now Aurisina) and Trieste. On 19 June, it was reported that Italian dirigibles had bombarded an Austrian ammunition factory near Trieste; and a naval battery shelled enemy batteries near Duino, north of Trieste (“Italians Raid by Air, Austrians by Sea,” New York Times [20 June 1915]: 2). Conditions in Trieste deteriorated as Italian shops were sacked and Italian residents were carried off or killed (“Saved by American Consul,” New York Times [22 June 1915]: 3). In late June, massive Austrian reinforcements concentrated around Trieste as Italian troops under General Luigi Cadorna continued to press forward all along the Isonzo River (New York Evening World [25 June 1915]: 2). Despite early successes and a numerical advantage, the Italian offensive eventually failed in what came to be known as the First Battle of the Isonzo.

Harriet Shaw Weaver (1876–1961), editor of The Egoist, published A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man in that magazine beginning 2 February 1914. JJ wrote her on 30 June 1915 to announce his arrival in Zurich and to inquire about A Portrait’s serial run (LI 82). James B. Pinker was Joyce’s literary agent in London; see JJ to Pound, 3 April 1915, notes. JJ wrote Pinker a postcard on 30 June 1915, asking “what news there is about my books” (LII 349).

Grant Richards published Dubliners in London in June 1914. In April 1915, Richards sent Joyce an account showing that total sales of Dubliners, including copies that Joyce himself had bought, stood at 461. Joyce’s contract with Richards provided that no royalties would be paid for the first 500 copies. See JJ to Pound, 7 May 1915, notes.

Before Italy joined the war, Joyce in Trieste (then part of the Austro-Hungarian empire) was able to use the address of his friend Italo Svevo’s father-in-law in Murano, near Venice, for forwarding of mail in either direction.

Before leaving for Zurich, JJ had been corresponding with B.W. Huebsch of New York, the eventual American publisher of Dubliners, and H.L. Mencken, editor of the literary magazine Smart Set, based in New York, which printed two Dubliners stories in May 1915 (see JJ to Pound, 19 April 1915, notes). Grant Richards wrote JJ on 12 and 26 April 1915 to say that no American edition of Dubliners had been arranged for, despite JJ’s impression that the book was being published at that time in the United States (Robert Scholes, “Grant Richard to James Joyce,” Studies in Bibliography, vol. 16 [1963]: 156-58).

The serialization of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man concluded with The Egoist, vol. 2, no. 9 (1 September 1915). It was first published as a book in 1916 by B.W. Huebsch in New York. The Egoist Press published the first English edition the following year.

Begun in the spring of 1914, Exiles was published in May 1918 by Grant Richards in London and by B.W. Huebsch in New York. It was first performed in a German translation in Munich in 1919. Joyce initially conceived Ulysses as a short story in 1906 but reconceived it as a much larger work blended with many of the persons from Dubliners when he returned to it eight or nine years later. It was first published in book form on 2 February 1922 by Shakespeare and Company in Paris. In October 1922, the Egoist Press in London published the first English edition from plates of the Paris edition.
